Excellencies, our quest for the total and unequivocal decolonization of the BVI continues and is at a critical stage. We are currently in the process of negotiating a new constitution with the United Kingdom. The official negotiations kicked off in August with the first round of talks. which was followed by a second round in September. The deliberations have been constructive thus far, and my meetings with the new UK Overseas Territories Minister, Uma Kumar, have been constructive. Another round of negotiations is anticipated in the weeks ahead, while technical and political discussions continue in the intervening period. Devolution of authority will be an important marker of progress. The objective is to agree a new constitution by the end of the year that meets the BVI's aspirations. My government is seeking what has been described as a pre-independence constitution that provides for full internal self-government, a bicameral legislature, and a pathway to full sovereignty. Please permit me to set out for you the key constitutional provisions we have proposed. The Premier should chair cabinet instead of a UK-appointed governor. This is already the case in other British overseas territories, such as Gibraltar and Bermuda, and also in the Crown dependencies. A Senate should be created to establish a bicameral legislature. This is already the case in Bermuda. Responsibility for the public service should be devolved to the elected arm of government under the authority of a minister instead of a UK-appointed governor. This is currently the case in the Crown dependencies and practically in Bermuda and Gibraltar. Responsibility for internal security should be devolved to the elected arm of government under the authority of a minister instead of a UK-appointed governor. The current delegated areas of external affairs should also be devolved to the elected arm of government, which is already the case in practice. There should be a defined pathway to full sovereignty in which the people of the Virgin Islands exercise their right to self-determination. Excellencies, friends, these are the core constitutional proposals the BVI is negotiating. The UK has also introduced its own proposals, which are points for further discussion in the negotiations. As a matter of principle, we also believe the unilateral authority of the United Kingdom to suspend or remove the democratic rights of the people of the BVI should be eliminated altogether, even if just on moral grounds. Progressing the territory along the path of self-determination is an international obligation of the UK under Article 73 of the UN Charter. The Decolonisation Commission will help to ensure the public is aware of the obligations and responsibilities of independence so that this option is approached in a responsible manner. My government has no doubt that as a country we would thrive. The BVI is grateful to this Committee and the C24 for your steadfast support. We greatly appreciate the understanding and solidarity of nations across Africa, Europe, the Middle East, Asia, the Pacific, and Latin America. Chair, ladies and gentlemen, members of the Fourth Committee, Excellencies, The United Nations Charter calls upon the administering power to transmit information on non-self-governing territories. This obligation allows the United Nations to follow the situation using official data. Article 73e provides for the regular communication to the Secretary-General of statistical and technical information pertaining to the economic, social and educational situation of these territories. Mr. Chair, Excellencies, members of the First Committee, your honor. In 1963, France established its nuclear testing center in our islands. Within a decade, a largely self-sufficient society became one built on consumerism, structurally dependent on transfer from the French state. Over time, the subsidized public sector drew capital and labor from the rest of the economy, harming our productive industries as our people left the lagoons and the fields. In 1962, our export covered 42% of our imports. Today, barely 5%. We import three-quarters of our food and almost all our energy. Three decades after the test ended, in 1996, the legacy remains. Our statute may say we control our economic policies. In practice, we have far less room for maneuver than a fully autonomous country. We have no control over monetary policy. Our currency is the CFP franc, once the franc of the French colonies of the Pacific, is issued in Paris and pegged to the euro. Without monetary tools, our governments have had to rely on fiscal policy alone. Yet our fiscal system was itself shaped by France. To attract civil servants to our islands, France maintained an income tax-free haven and doubled their salaries. that legacy have proved nearly impossible to challenge, despite the various changes in our political statute. Under political pressure to keep the status quo, our governments have kept funding public services, mainly through indirect taxation. Such taxation deepens inequality, hinders our exports, and drives up the cost of living. The data bear this out. Prices are 31% higher than in France. Our Gini coefficient, last updated over a decade ago, places our income inequality well above France and above independent neighbors such as Fiji. We all seek a sustainable, equitable, climate-resilient economy. It cannot be achieved without the levers of a sovereign state. Without political emancipation, there can be no economic emancipation. We therefore ask this committee to recognize these facts and to support our people in gaining the means to build an economy that reflects the aspiration. Thank you, Marudu.

My 25th autumn in this room, a quarter of a century. When I first came here in 2002, I was 30 years old. I sat behind the great Sir Joe Bossano. I did not say a word. I listened and I learnt. 25 years on, having addressed you 15 times, I speak to you for the last time as Chief Minister of Gibraltar. And I do so in a year that history will not let us ignore. Because this December, it will be 80 years since Gibraltar was first placed on the United Nations list of non-self-governing territories. 80 years. Four Chief Ministers of Gibraltar have come before the United Nations to make our people's case in that time. Sir Joshua Hassan came first, in 1963, to tell you that Gibraltar is ours. Sir Joe Bosano brought us back in 1992. He promised we would keep coming until you acted on our freely expressed wishes as a people. Sir Peter Caruana rightly told you for 16 years that you should treat the self-determination of our people as paramount. And I have addressed you as leader of the opposition in 2011 and as Chief Minister every year I could since to tell you the same thing in my own words. Eight decades on your list. Six decades of speeches. Four successive leaders. One consistent message. because the international legal principles governing our decolonization have not changed, and neither have we. So let me state the law plainly one last time. Article 73 of the Charter makes the interests of the inhabitants of a non-self-governing territory paramount, not the interests of any neighbor or of any claimant. Only the people of a territory. Us, the people of Gibraltar. Article 1 of both international covenants, extended to Gibraltar 50 years ago, declares that all peoples have the right to self-determination. Resolution 1514 also says all peoples, not some, all peoples. Resolution 1541 says the obligation to transmit information in respect of a territory applies when the territory is separate and distinct from its administering power. A state that merely claims such a territory and has no legal ties of territorial sovereignty with it has no standing in its decolonization. And the International Court of Justice in the cases of Namibia and Western Sahara and in its Chagos opinion of 2019 has made these principles clear. The right of self-determination is the governing principle of decolonization. It requires the free and genuine expression of the will of the people concerned. And the international community as a whole has an obligation to ensure that the right is fulfilled. Territorial integrity, properly understood as a shield for colonized people. It is not a sword in the hands of expansionist neighbors, whether in Southern Europe, South America, or elsewhere. What stands against all of our unbeatable legal arguments? nothing but the resolutions of the 1960s, resolutions procured by a murderous dictator whose legacy democratic Spain has rightly left behind. And the people of Gibraltar have spoken. In 1967, 99% of us chose not to pass under Spanish sovereignty. In 2002, 99% of us rejected shared sovereignty with Spain. We have been asked and we have been clear and unequivocal in our answer. All we await is for you to hear our answer and to start acting in keeping with the clearly expressed wishes of the people of Gibraltar. Chair, since I last addressed you, something important has changed. The treaty between the United Kingdom and the European Union in respect of Gibraltar has now been signed and is being provisionally applied. It was negotiated at our request and with my government leading for our people at the table. removed a short but no less cruel iron curtain that General Franco drew closed to divide families and friends. And our treaty states in terms that nothing in it affects the positions of sovereignty of each of the parties. So understand what we have done. We have removed the barbed wire and the chain-link fence, but we have not wavered on our sacrosanct sovereignty. We have shown that our people can build friendship with our neighbor without surrendering a single one of our rights. Cooperation we welcome, but we will never capitulate. And so, Chair, Direct the C-24 to send a visiting mission to Gibraltar. Let them come and see a self-governing, democratic, prosperous people, confident in who we are and confident in our rights. And then do what the charter requires. Recommend our removal from the list. Chair, I was born in 1972. behind a frontier closed by a military dictator to seek to break our democratic will. But it did not break our will. My parents' generation kept our country alive. My generation built it into a modern nation. And our children's generation will inherit that nation with clearly established inalienable rights. I came to this room first as a young man who listened avidly. I leave it as a father who speaks passionately with children who understand clearly, because you can keep us on the list of non-self-governing territories, you can pretend that institutional inertia in the C24 excuses you from acting, but you cannot deny us our right to self-determination. You may outlast this Chief Minister, but you will never outlast the people of Gibraltar. And let me give you some advice. After 80 years, it's time that you wake up and smell the coffee. Gibraltar belongs only to the Gibraltarians. It always has, and it always will. Thank you, Chair, and goodbye for now.

I thank the Chief Minister. Does any member wish to ask a question to the Chief Minister of Gibraltar or comment on his statement? There are no requests for the floor. We will now listen to one petitioner on the question of Gibraltar. I invite Mr. Richard Butigieg to take a seat at the petitioner's table. You have the floor, sir.

Afternoon, Mr. Chairman and distinguished members of the committee. Thank you for giving me the opportunity to address you once again. I have stood before this committee many times over the years. I have spoken about our history, about democracy, and of course, our right to self-determination. Today, however, I want to speak about what is possible when people choose to work together. In 2026, after years of difficult negotiation, Gibraltar, the United Kingdom and the European Union reached agreement on a new framework for Gibraltar's relationship within the European Union. I believe that agreement carries an important lesson for this Committee, because the agreement shows that when people sit around a table in good faith, listen to one another and truly look for practical solutions, they can achieve things that once seemed extremely difficult, if not impossible. But there is still one part of Gibraltar's story which remains unresolved, and that is that Gibraltar remains on the United Nations list of non-self-governing territories. And I have to ask, after all these years, what exactly is the United Nations waiting for? The people of Gibraltar have built democratic institutions. We govern ourselves. We take responsibility for our own affairs, and generation after generation of Gibraltarians have made their wishes known. Yet, we remain on a list created more than 70 years ago. Mr. Chairman, that list is supposed to reflect reality, but when reality changes, surely the list must change too. That is why I make the same invitation that I have made many times before: send a visiting mission once and for all. And then ask yourselves whether the description of Gibraltar on that list still reflects the Gibraltar that exists today. I am not asking this Committee to take anyone's side. I am asking it to look, to listen, and above all, to act. There is a generation growing up which should not have to inherit a question that has remained unresolved for decades before them. The recent agreement in relation to Brexit has shown us that progress is possible, so perhaps now is the time for the United Nations to show that they too can progress and complete the UN work that remains unfinished. If there is something more that Gibraltar must do, we deserve to know what it is. And if there is not, then surely the time has come to act. Mr. Chairman, I do not want to stand before this committee year after year repeating the same words, but I or others will continue to do so because the next generation must be able to look back at all of you and say they finally listened, they finally came, and they finally finished the job.

Thank you.

I thank the petitioner. Ladies and gentlemen, we will now turn to the question of Guam. The Lieutenant Governor of Guam, Mr. Joshua Tenorio, wishes to make a statement on behalf of the Governor of Guam, Her Excellency, Lou Leon Guerrero. In accordance with established procedure, I propose that the committee invite the Lieutenant Governor of Guam to make a statement. It is so decided. As such, I invite the Lieutenant Governor of Guam, Mr. Joshua Mr. Norio to take a seat at the committee's table. You have the floor sir for up to 7 minutes.

Half a day. Half a day, your excellent, let's see. Hafadai, Your Excellency, Chairman Sec and distinguished members of the committee. Guam's people are committed to the stewardship of our lands and waters and to the wellbeing and prosperity of our people, especially our youth and elders. We remain committed to a peaceful and informed process of self-determination, consistent with the principles of the charter and the freely expressed will of the people. The path forward, however, must acknowledge the distinct history of the Chamorro people, the indigenous people of Guam, and the historical injustices they have experienced. And the United States has an obligation to address and resolve this history. Guam has long occupied a strategic position in the Pacific, and our people have long borne the consequences of global conflict and geopolitical competition. most profoundly through the tremendous loss of life, displacement, and hardship during the occupation and liberation of Guam in the Second World War. More than eight decades of United States military land use have left an environmental legacy that includes unexploded ordnance, former military disposal sites, and contamination of soil and groundwater. Anderson Air Force Base remains a United States Environmental Protection Agency Superfund site requiring long-term remediation, while PFAS and other persistent contaminants present additional concerns. An active investigation is also determining the cause of dieldrin contamination affecting water wells serving northern residents near the base. These issues are especially significant on a small island with finite land and freshwater resources. Much of the United States military presence in Northern Guam sits above the Northern Guam Lens Aquifer, our principal source of drinking water. In 2021, United Nations Special Rapporteurs warned of a direct risk to the health of local populations and expressed concern about Guam's principal source of drinking water. The draft resolution similarly recalls concerns that the military buildup could cause additional and irreparable harm to Guam's land and marine environments. At the same time, we recognize that the United States presence has long been an important source of economic stability for Guam. Expenditures by our administering power support employment, household incomes, local businesses, and infrastructure, while the current defense buildup is generating significant economic activity and expanding Guam's tax base. Yet, this growth has also placed significant pressure on housing costs and affordability for Guam's working families. Over the past decade, more than 8.7 billion U.S. dollars in military construction and modernization associated with the U.S. Marine Corps relocation and related defense infrastructure has been managed on Guam, financed by the United States Congress and contributions from the government of Japan. Additional investment is underway for missile defense and other military infrastructure. These contributions are substantial, but Guam should not have to choose between economic opportunity, security, and environmental protection. Sustainable development requires that these objectives advance together. As investment in Guam's strategic role grows, so too should investment in environmental remediation, safe drinking water, resilient civilian infrastructure, and the long-term health of our community. Significant legacy remediation remains unfinished and should be prioritized by the United States together with policies that enable greater economic self-sufficiency. Too often, decisions in Washington affecting Guam are made without our input. Legislation is being proposed in the United States Congress to establish a regular formal process of consultation between the government of Guam and the United States. Such a process can help ensure that Guam's views are considered when decisions affecting our land, economy, and people are made. That principle must extend to our ocean. The United States is advancing a process to lease areas of the outer continental shelf near the Mariana Islands for exploration and possible future development of critical mineral resources. While the current action does not itself authorize commercial mining, it represents a significant step toward potential mineral development in our region's deep ocean. Guam's leadership is united and has called for a halt to the advancement of seabed mineral leasing in the waters surrounding the Marianas until adequate scientific study, environmental review, and meaningful consultation with our people have occurred. This is also why Guam must make greater use of the international forums available to us on oceans, climate, and sustainable development. We have seen what greater participation can accomplish. In 2024, Guam was accepted as an associate member of the Pacific Islands Forum, and in 2025, we took our place for the first time in that capacity alongside the leaders of our Pacific region to address sea level rise and other shared regional concerns. Guam is ready to make fuller use of these opportunities to take our rightful place in regional and international discussions, contribute our experience, and work with others on the challenges and opportunities we share. The draft resolution on Guam gives this committee an opportunity to affirm the importance of our environment, our economy, and our participation. We ask you to support its calls for sustainable and equitable development, environmental restoration and protection, and continued attention to the impacts of militarization. We renew our request for a visiting mission to assess the situation in Guam. Our people seek a future in which our economy can grow, our lands and waters are protected, our indigenous heritage is respected, and Guam can participate meaningfully in discussions and decisions that affect our island. That future depends upon responsible stewardship, genuine partnership, recognition of our history, and above all, respect for the right of the people of Guam to shape their own future. and thank you.

I thank the Lieutenant Governor of Guernsey. Does any member wish to put questions to the Lieutenant Governor or comment on his statement? No delegation is asking for the floor. We shall now hear the petitioners wishing to make statements on the question of Guam. I invite the first petitioner to take the floor, Mr. Bryan Aguan.

Half a day, Mr. Chairman, and all the members of the committee. I'm indigenous Chamorro son of Guam. I reflect on the numerous Chamorro petitioners and our allies who have paved the way for this opportunity to petition on behalf of Guam. Their legacy continues on as an integral part of our quest towards genuine act of self-determination and decolonization. Guam's administering power, the United States is celebrating 250 years as an independent country, allowing some principles of freedom, democracy, and equality. Although notable, the United States continues to subjugate Guam and her people to an inferior inequitable non-self-governing status, depriving Guam of the very principles it espouses. At the center of Guam's quest for decolonization are the indigenous Chamorro people and the exercise of their fundamental human right of self-determination. The United States has chosen to be a non-cooperative actor in the facilitation of Chamorro self-determination. The United States is seemingly content with only allowing Guam a limited form of self-government and our people conditional United States citizenship. This is unquestionably short of a full measure of self-government. is in the best interest of the United States to maintain the political status quo for Guam, is in their best interest to maintain control over Guam's affairs without our people's free, prior, and informed consent, is in their best interest to perpetuate systemic inequities that has displaced tens of thousands of Chamorros, resulting in the Chamorro people becoming a minority in their own homeland. The governor of Guam established the framework for the Chamorro people to vote in a political-sized puppet site. The United States asserted that a vote led primarily by the Chamorro people, excuse me, violated the United States Constitution and the voting rights of American citizens. This is a blatant violation of the United States obligation through the UN Charter to take due account of political aspirations of the peoples and to assist them the progressive development of their free political institutions according to the particular circumstances of each territory and its peoples. The United States has willfully misrepresented the peoples in Guam's case through the weaponization of universal suffrage as a method to erase Chamorro people. The exercise of Chamorro self-determination should not be defined by the United States. It has been recognized indigenous peoples have the right to the full enjoyment as a collective or as individuals of all human rights and fundamental freedoms as recognized in the Charter of the United Nations, Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and International Human Rights Law. Self-determination is an inherent human right that the Chamorro people must exercise with dignity and without burden to begin the actual of a full measure of self-government for Guam. I formally request for a United Nations visiting mission to Guam. A visiting mission will be beneficial for members of the answer community to attain an informed perspective, the United States irresponsibility and their obligation to resolve Guam's colonial plight. I formally request the members of this committee assist Guam in elevating the issue of Chamorro self-determination through appropriate human rights institutions. This will serve as a necessary reckoning for the United States to pay restitution to the Chamorro people, who have endured colonization for over 500 years. Thank you, Mr. Chair.
I thank the petitioner for that statement. I now give the floor to Pim Limtiaco.

My name is Pinlim Tiako, and I am a native Chamorro from Guam. I would like to thank and acknowledge all distinguished members of the fourth committee for having me here. There is possibly one word to summarize our current situation, sick. We are sick of the continued colonization of our lands and waters by the US. We have been getting sick from the continued contamination and damage of our water sources. And we find the situation sick that we have been ignored in the deep sea mining discussions by the US federal government. The US already occupies one third of our island for its military base operations. And once again, our people have yet to receive the land back from the federal government since World War II. These bases have knowingly contaminated our primary water sources for decades with dieldrin, a banned insecticide that is known to cause cancer and reproductive issues. Residents who live closely to them continue to suffer from chronic and fatal health conditions caused by this environmental exposure. The deep-sea mining situation continues to be a threat to our livelihood, Indigenous practice, and marine biodiversity across the Pacific. The U.S. plans to lease over 67 million acres of seafloor around our island to mining companies. Even after passing local legislation and holding peaceful gatherings against these measures, the U.S. federal government has still decided to hold the lease sale by December 16, 2026. The Trump administration heeded the will of our people on this issue. Instead, it expedited the timeline and expanded the area it was going to lease. Our current political status as a territory continues to prevent us from having any autonomy to protect our environment. This is already my fifth time here for the past nine years, and I once again urge the Fourth Committee to take action to conduct a visiting mission to Guam to study the effects, and more importantly, to fulfill its goal to eradicate colonialism. I would also like to empower the Fourth Committee to summon the International Seabed Authority to implement its power to organize, regulate, and control all mineral resource-related activities for the benefit of humankind as a whole. If your children were sick, would you ignore their cries for help? Would you take away their resources to stay alive? Would you knowingly poison them until it is too late to intervene? Does hearing what our people have been going through for centuries make you sick? Thank you for your time.

I thank the petitioner.

I now give the floor to Maya Fino.

My name is Maya Fino from the Center for Constitutional Rights, and I'm reading testimony by Jonita Kerr and Monica Flores of Putehigwa Han in Guam who could not attend today's meeting. Members of Putehigwa Han traveled almost 8,000 miles and around 24 hours to Washington, DC this past Saturday to come to the US Supreme Court, the highest court in the country, to hold the Air Force accountable to following the National Environmental Policy Act, or NEPA, which has a heightened importance in Guam, where the US military occupies more than a quarter of the island, while the people of Guam lack political power as a US military colony. The NEPA review is often the only structured opportunity for the community in Guam to participate in the federal decision-making process for federal projects and proposals that have lasting impacts on health, well-being, environment, and the cultural heritage of the indigenous Chamorro people. This is not merely a bureaucratic process, but the primary way for the federal government to be held accountable and listen to the people who are forced to live with the consequences of their decisions and actions. Simultaneously, decisions about deep sea mining are being made without consent and again without political or social equity. Harming ocean ecosystems ultimately impacts community well-being, climate resilience, cultural survival, food security, spiritual practices, and is an attack on the sovereignty of all Indigenous Pacific communities. According to the Trump administration, who is fast tracking deep sea mining in advance of international law, the targeting of the minerals is for the economic prosperity and security of the United States at the cost of the Marianas archipelago. The people of Guam understand that there is no public benefit to the permanent and irreversible destruction of the ocean ecosystem, which they have been a part of for almost 4,000 years. Meanwhile, these minerals will be used to greatly enrich those who have no regard for the health and welfare of the people of the Marianas, and to develop weapons and AI tech for never-ending cycles of war and war games. Protehi Guahan humbly implores an international intervention and alleviation to non-stop war games that exacerbate threats to climate resilience, the colonial resource grabbing through deep sea mining, and an end to military destruction and aggression in our lands and waters. Thank you, Nsizu Usmasi.
I thank the petitioner. I give the floor. I give the floor to Melvin Benny One Pat. Bonjour.

After your Excellency, Chairman, and honorable members of the committee. My name is Melvin Wampat Borja. I'm the executive director of the Commission on Decolonization. In 2016, the UN General Assembly's resolution on the question of Guam has recognized that the incessant militarization of Guam is the most acute threat to the legitimate exercise of our island's decolonization. A decade later, the continued and growing presence of the United States military on Guam is indeed an impediment to the actualization of the political desires of the native inhabitants of Guam and the indigenous the Chamorro people. It is an understatement to say that the United States national security interests take precedence over the social, political, and economic aspirations of our people. The emphasis placed on Guam's strategic location in the Pacific region and its inequitable political status have endowed our administering power with unilateral control and sovereignty to create a situation in which their security and defense priorities come at the expense of local interests and concerns. The people of Guam, most especially the indigenous Chamorro people, have borne undue costs to our culture, language, environment, and economy, all while living in an inequitable political status that robs us of the ability to consent to military activities that cause genuine harm and create a perception of the island to be both a target and asset to external powers. Nearly one-third of Guam's landmass has been used by our administering power for military purposes, taken predominantly from indigenous Chamorro families. There is a longstanding request to our administering power to continue to transfer land to the original land owners of the territory to continue to recognize and respect the political rights and the cultural and ethnic identity of the CHamoru people of Guam. Though we welcome these efforts, it is of particular concern that our administering power is now seeking the acquisition of 2,400 housing units outside of military controlled properties. These units will accommodate an estimated 10,000 new military personnel and their dependents. This demand is well above our island's capacity and places our people in direct competition for housing, creating another factor that will cause the further displacement of the Chamorro people from their homeland. Guam is more than just a strategic location. It is an island that has been stewarded by a 4,000 year old civilization that predated colonialism by our administering power. We request a United Nations visiting mission as an actionable and reasonable step which must be taken to provide an updated understanding of the situation in Guam. And thank you, Mr. Chairman, for this opportunity.
I thank the petitioner. I now give the floor to Harmony Dorilisa Palengtas.

Good afternoon, Mr. Chair and honorable members of the fourth committee. As a non-self-governing territory, the people of Guam shoulder an environmental burden that directly harms our overall wellbeing and capacities for advancement. A 2021 United Nations Special Rapporteur report expressed concern on the association between military escalation and the risk of contamination. Today, we are living with the impacts they first saw. In September, work by an independent nonprofit media organization uncovered historical records unsafe levels of dieldrin on Anderson Air Force Base. In connection, families from the village of Yigo are facing the reality of decades-long exposure to a toxic pesticide through the contamination of finite freshwater resources. Past and present activities conducted by the United States military in the pursuit of their national security interest have come at the cost of protecting and preserving the lands, airs, and waters of Guam. This committee should be concerned that our administering power has claimed an exclusive right to use and extract resources from the island and surrounding waters without consent from the community, most especially the indigenous Tamoro people. As recognized by the United Nations, indigenous peoples have the right to redress for the lands, territories, and resources which they have traditionally owned or otherwise occupied or used, and which have been confiscated, taken, occupied, used, or damaged without their free, prior, and informed consent. The exploitive and extractive nature of the United States military must be altered to undo harms and ensure future actions respect the rights of the Chamorro people. If the United States is to uphold their obligation to aid in the development of self-government and actualization of the political aspirations of the native inhabitants of Guam, inviting genuine partnership to address environmental harms is a step in the right direction. Consulting local counterparts, asking not only for comments but consent from the people are ways in which you involve the community that is connected to these issues. In addition, providing funding to prevent and mitigate environmental degradation due to military activities is crucial. If billions of dollars can be placed into building a military installation, then funding should exist to ensure that toxic chemicals do not pollute the largest freshwater resource in the island. I also ask for the committee's support in these efforts. A United Nations visiting mission would provide for an updated understanding of the situation in Guam and the obstacles to achieving full self-government. Earnest collaboration with our administering power and the international community can change the trajectory of Guam's future. I invite you to be part of that journey.

I thank the petitioner. Ladies and gentlemen, we have heard the last petitioner on the question of Guam. And we have reached the end of our allotted time.
